title: Cloud Firestore
objectives: Understand Firestore via a real-life analogy
Manage cost — reads are the dominant driver

sections.markdown:
**Think of Firestore as a globally-distributed filing cabinet with live-updating drawers.**

- Every **drawer** is a **collection** (e.g., 'users', 'orders').
- Every **folder** inside a drawer is a **document** — max 1 MiB, JSON-like structured data.
- Folders can themselves contain **sub-drawers** (subcollections) → nested arbitrarily deep.
- Every folder has a **unique label** (docId) — either you choose it or Firestore auto-assigns.

**The magic:** the filing cabinet is replicated to **DOZENS of data centers across the world** with 99.999% availability. When you write, it commits to a majority + fans out. When you read, you hit the nearest replica in milliseconds. **AND** — you can subscribe to a folder or a filter (`.snapshots()`) and get **live push updates** every time anything changes. Zero polling. Perfect for chat, dashboards, collaborative editing, live leaderboards.

**The catch (this shapes everything):** Firestore charges **per document READ, WRITE, and DELETE**. Not per query — per document RETURNED. A screen that fetches 200 documents on every navigation → 200 reads × 100 users/day × 30 days = 600K reads/month → **$$$**. **A poorly designed screen can be 100× more expensive than a well-designed one.** This is why Firestore experts obsess over pagination, caching, denormalization, and query design.

**Serverless — no ops.** Google shards, replicates, indexes, backs up, and scales it for you. You just define collections + rules and write client code.

**When to use Firestore:** apps needing real-time sync (chat, dashboards, collaborative), user-scoped mostly-write-shallow data, teams without a backend crew, MVP → 10M users without ops. **When NOT:** complex relational joins, analytics workloads (use BigQuery), extreme high-frequency writes to a single doc (hotspot).

**This topic is the highest-leverage backend skill for Firebase-first Flutter/mobile developers.** Every mobile interview at Firebase-shop companies (Duolingo, Alibaba, NYT, Airbnb Design) grills Firestore modeling + cost.

**Cloud Firestore** is Google's serverless, globally-distributed, real-time NoSQL document database. Data lives in **collections of documents** (max 1 MiB each; JSON-like maps of fields). Queries return one-time snapshots or **live Streams**. Access is enforced by **Security Rules** (declarative, server-side). Costs: **reads, writes, deletes, storage, egress** — reads dominate for most apps. Free tier: 50K reads / 20K writes / 20K deletes / 1 GB storage per day. Perfect for real-time collaborative apps.
## Data model — collections + documents

**Rules of the model:**

- Document max **1 MiB** — big blobs go in Cloud Storage; link via URL.
- Field name max **1500 bytes**, path max **6144 bytes**.
- Nested map/array depth max **20 levels**.
- Subcollections don't inherit rules or fields from parent — they're independent.
- **No joins.** Denormalize. Duplicate hot fields (`user.displayName` on each message) to avoid N+1 queries.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: `.get()` on every navigation.** Cache locally, use `Source.cache` for repeat views. Firestore reads add up FAST.
**Mistake 2: OFFSET pagination.** Firestore charges reads for skipped documents. Use cursor-based `startAfterDocument`.
**Mistake 3: Fully normalized schema.** No joins in Firestore — you'll fire N+1 queries. Denormalize; embed hot fields.
**Mistake 4: Monotonic doc IDs.** Sequential IDs (timestamps, UUIDv1) → single-shard hotspot → high tail latency. Use auto-IDs or random prefixes.
**Mistake 5: Trusting client for data validity.** Rules can enforce shape + type checks. Do it.
**Mistake 6: Ignoring composite index prompts.** Firestore will ERROR; the error message contains a link that auto-creates the index. Click it.
**Mistake 7: Real-time listener leaks.** `snapshots().listen()` without `.cancel()` on disposal → ghost reads → cost + battery.
**Mistake 8: Deleting parent doc, subcollections orphaned.** Use recursive delete via Cloud Function or admin CLI.
## Best practices
**1. Denormalize.** Embed hot fields; duplicate is fine. Firestore ≠ SQL.
**2. Cursor pagination.** `startAfterDocument`; never OFFSET.
**3. Cache-first for repeat reads.** `Source.cache` on unchanged data.
**4. Rules validate + authorize.** Type check, shape check, ownership check.
**5. Composite indexes proactively.** Deploy `firestore.indexes.json`; don't wait for prod errors.
**6. Atomic ops for concurrent updates.** `FieldValue.increment`, `arrayUnion`, `arrayRemove` — no read-modify-write bugs.
**7. `serverTimestamp()`, not client clock.** Immune to device time drift.
**8. Dispose listeners.** `.cancel()` in `dispose()`. Always.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy) — Todo app.** CRUD todos scoped by userId; real-time list.
**Practice 2 (Medium) — Chat.** `chats/{chatId}/messages` subcollection; real-time; ordered by timestamp.
**Practice 3 (Medium) — Composite index.** Query with two `where` + `orderBy` → observe index prompt → create → verify.
**Practice 4 (Hard) — Rules ownership + custom claims.** Owner-only writes; admin override via role claim.
**Practice 5 (Hard) — Batch + transaction.** Order checkout: create order + decrement inventory + update user — atomic.
**Practice 6 (Expert) — Cost audit.** Instrument every screen; log read count; find + fix the most expensive.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: Firestore data model and cost model?**

**A:** **Data model:** hierarchical — collections contain documents; documents contain fields OR subcollections; nested arbitrarily. Documents max 1 MiB, JSON-like. NO JOINS. Data must be DENORMALIZED — duplicate hot fields (e.g., `user.name` on each message) so one query returns everything the UI needs. **Cost model:** you pay per document READ + WRITE + DELETE — NOT per query. A query returning 100 docs = 100 reads. Also pay for storage + egress. **Free tier:** 50K reads / 20K writes / 20K deletes / 1 GB / day. **Design implication:** pagination, caching, and denormalization DIRECTLY reduce cost. A screen that reads all 500 users on every navigation costs 100× more than one that reads 20 + caches. Real-world apps live or die on this — the difference between 'unaffordable at 10K MAU' and 'profitable at 1M MAU' is usually design choices in the first two weeks.

**Q2: How do you avoid hotspots in Firestore?**

**A:** A hotspot is a range of doc IDs or index entries that gets a burst of writes — Firestore serializes writes per range → high tail latency + throttling. **Sources:** (1) **Monotonic IDs** (timestamps, UUIDv1, sequential counters) → all inserts go to the same tail range. Fix: use auto-generated IDs OR prepend a high-cardinality prefix. (2) **Frequently-incremented counter** on a single doc → 1 write/sec limit per doc. Fix: **distributed counters** — shard the counter into N documents, sum on read. (3) **Same-user writes cascading** — a Function that fires on every user login and writes back to their doc. **The 1-write-per-second-per-doc soft cap** is the real number to remember. Detect hotspots via **Cloud Monitoring / Cloud Firestore stats** or slow-write reports in the console. This is one of the top questions in Firebase-shop interviews.

**Q3: When are composite indexes required?**

**A:** Firestore auto-indexes every single field. But queries combining MULTIPLE fields (multiple `where` + `orderBy`, or a range `where` on one field + `orderBy` on a different one) need a **composite index**. Example: `where('status', '==', 'paid').where('total', '>', 100).orderBy('createdAt')` needs an index on `(status, total, createdAt)`. **First time you run such a query, Firestore ERRORS with a link that auto-creates the index in the console.** Best practice: don't wait for prod — declare indexes in `firestore.indexes.json`, commit to git, deploy via `firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes`. **Cost:** indexes bloat storage + write cost — every write updates every relevant index. Delete unused ones. Also: **array-contains-any + in queries** have restrictions (max 10 items, one per query). **Every interview asks about composite indexes.**

**Q4: How do Security Rules work?**

**A:** Declarative access-control language deployed via `firebase deploy --only firestore:rules`. Runs on Google's servers for EVERY request — client CANNOT bypass. Syntax: `match /path/{wildcard} { allow read/write/create/update/delete: if <condition>; }`. Conditions use `request.auth.uid`, `request.auth.token.<claim>`, `resource.data.<field>` (existing doc), `request.resource.data.<field>` (incoming write). **Common patterns:** ownership (`request.auth.uid == resource.data.ownerId`), role via custom claim (`request.auth.token.role == 'admin'`), immutable fields (`request.resource.data.createdAt == resource.data.createdAt`), type/shape validation (`request.resource.data.total is number`). **Test with emulator + `@firebase/rules-unit-testing`.** **Default deny.** Every rule you don't write is a leak — always end with `match /{doc=**} { allow read, write: if false; }`. **This is THE security layer of a Firebase app.**

**Q5: What's the difference between batched writes and transactions?**

**A:** **Batched writes** — group up to 500 write ops (set/update/delete) into ONE atomic commit. No reads. Use for related writes that should all succeed or fail together. **Example:** create order + update user's order count + delete cart in ONE batch. **Transactions** — atomic read-then-write. Read documents inside the tx, compute values, write back. Firestore uses OPTIMISTIC CONCURRENCY: if any of the read docs changed between read and write, tx retries automatically (up to 5x). **Example:** decrement inventory only if `stock > 0`. **Rules:** transactions can hold up to 500 doc references; batched writes can have 500 ops. Transactions retry on conflict; batches don't. **When to choose:** if you need to read-then-write conditionally → transaction. Just multiple writes → batch (cheaper, no retries). **Both are all-or-nothing atomic** — this is Firestore's answer to ACID.

**Q6: How do you minimize Firestore cost?**

**A:** **Reads dominate cost — that's the target.** (1) **Cache locally** — Firestore SDK's offline cache is free; use `Source.cache` for unchanged data. (2) **Pagination** — cursor-based, small page size (20-50). Never fetch a whole collection. (3) **Denormalize** — embed fields to avoid follow-up queries. (4) **Live listeners** are cheaper than repeated `.get()` for real-time data (only changes are read after initial snapshot). (5) **BUT** — listener leaks are EXPENSIVE; dispose them. (6) **Aggregation queries** (Firestore added `count`, `sum`, `avg` server-side) — instead of fetching + counting. (7) **Reduce document size** — split hot small fields from big ones. Firestore charges based on read, not size, but egress adds up. (8) **Use `select`** (via subcollections or field masks) to fetch only needed fields. (9) **Monitor via Cloud Monitoring** — set alerts on read spikes. **Cost = 90% of Firestore adoption failures.**

**Q7: When would you NOT choose Firestore?**

**A:** **(1) Complex relational joins** — Firestore has no joins. If your data is 5-table relational + heavy analytics, use Postgres or Cloud SQL. **(2) High-frequency writes to a single doc** — 1 write/sec soft cap; batch or shard. **(3) Very large per-user data volumes** — 1 MiB per doc + read costs; billing-heavy documents (audit logs, telemetry) belong in BigQuery. **(4) Full-text search** — Firestore only does prefix matching; use Algolia or Typesense for real search. **(5) Analytics workloads** — BigQuery is the answer; even export Firestore → BigQuery via extension. **(6) Multi-region strong consistency** — Firestore is eventually consistent across regions; if you need strict serializability across continents, Spanner. **(7) Very cost-sensitive read-heavy** — reads add up; sometimes RTDB (bandwidth-priced) is cheaper. **The senior skill is knowing WHICH backend fits.** Firestore is amazing for real-time collaborative + user-scoped data; wrong for OLAP.

## Real-world usage

- **Chats + collaborative apps** — Firestore's real-time listeners are the go-to.
- **Duolingo, Alibaba, NYT, Fabulous, Airbnb Design** — all Firebase-first.
- **Startup MVPs → 1M users** — no backend team needed.
- **Multi-tenant SaaS** — `tenants/{tid}/{doc=**}` pattern + custom claims.
- **Games** — leaderboards, saves, friend feeds.
- **NOT for** — OLAP (BigQuery), full-text search (Algolia), high-throughput single-doc writes.

## Advanced notes

- **Distributed counters** — shard a counter into N docs; sum on read; write to random shard.
- **`FieldValue.increment(1)`** — atomic, but 1 write/sec/doc cap.
- **Aggregation queries** — `count`, `sum`, `avg` server-side (added 2023).
- **Bundles** — pre-computed query results served from Firebase Hosting CDN → free reads for cached queries.
- **Datastore mode vs Native mode** — Datastore mode = strongly consistent global writes but no real-time listeners; Native = real-time + eventual multi-region.
- **Emulator suite** — `firebase emulators:start`; test rules + queries offline.
- **BigQuery export** — extension exports every change to BigQuery for analytics.
- **Cloud Functions triggers** — `onCreate`, `onUpdate`, `onDelete` on any collection.
- **Firestore TTL** — auto-delete docs after N seconds (via `expireAt` field + TTL policy).
- **App Check** — attests client is legitimate.
- **Chunked deletes** — deleting > 500 docs? Use Cloud Function or admin CLI's recursive delete.
- **Multi-DB** — Firestore now supports multiple named databases per project (2023).
- **Backup + restore** — scheduled exports to GCS.
- **Vector search** — Firestore added vector similarity queries (2024) for AI/RAG apps.
